nodes.rationale: Only email+password is offered because OTP/Google/Apple are Supabase project dashboard settings rather than application code; a button for a provider that is not enabled would just produce a confusing error. The error text never distinguishes 'no such account' from 'wrong password' because that difference tells an attacker which emails exist. router.refresh() before push so server components re-read the new session cookie.

nodes.label: Sign In Panel
nodes.rationale: Owns the email/password state so the demo panel can fill the form by setting state directly, with no prop-to-state syncing effect anywhere. When accounts is null the two-column grid collapses to the plain centred card and no demo code is reachable at all.

nodes.label: Sign Out Button
nodes.rationale: Signs out through the browser client because @supabase/ssr stores the session in cookies, so clearing it there clears what the server components read next request; router.refresh() forces those components to re-run against the now-empty session. The redirect happens even if signOut() fails, since a failure still leaves a stale cookie and the sign-in page re-checks for real. On operational screens it doubles as the account switcher, because the kitchen tablet and the manager's screen are often the same device.

nodes.label: Checkout Address Step
nodes.rationale: A plain server-action form with no client state, so it works before hydration. The `compact` prop lets the same form be reused inline inside the payment step rather than duplicating the address fields.

nodes.label: Checkout Auth Step
nodes.rationale: Account creation is placed late in checkout (PRD 6): the customer has already chosen and configured a plan, so they are asked for details in exchange for something concrete rather than as a toll gate on the way in. When email confirmation is enabled signUp returns no session, so it says so explicitly and promises the plan selection is saved, rather than leaving the customer on a page that will never advance.

nodes.label: Raw-Body-First Signature Verification
nodes.rationale: Both webhook routes call request.text() before any JSON parsing, because parsing and re-serialising would change the bytes the provider's HMAC was computed over and every signature would fail. Verification precedes all persistence: an unverified payload never becomes an order or a payment.

nodes.label: Webhook Idempotency on Provider Event Id
nodes.rationale: Replays must be harmless because every provider retries. Payments deduplicate by inserting into payment_events first and treating Postgres error 23505 (unique violation) as 'already processed' -- the unique index, not application logic, is what makes a replay a no-op. Marketplace pushes the same guarantee down into the ingestion RPCs, which are idempotent on the provider's own event and order ids.
nodes.norm_label: webhook idempotency on provider event id

nodes.label: Per-Provider Failure Isolation
nodes.rationale: An ingestion failure calls record_integration_failure with only that provider, tripping that provider's breaker alone. Swiggy, Zomato and the website share nothing but the KOT they eventually write to, so one integration going bad cannot stop the others taking orders.

nodes.label: Webhook Is Authoritative, Callback Is Cosmetic
nodes.rationale: The browser return-callback is a convenience for the customer's screen; the business trusts the server-to-server webhook because it arrives even when the customer closes the tab mid-payment. Both converge on the same idempotent confirm RPC so whichever wins the race, exactly one activation, credit grant and invoice results.
nodes.norm_label: webhook is authoritative, callback is cosmetic

nodes.label: Late Account Creation
nodes.rationale: PRD 6: no account is required to browse or configure a plan. The draft is held in a cookie and the auth step appears only at checkout, so signup is asked for in exchange for something concrete. The sign-in page repeats the promise: 'Buying a plan? You do not need an account first'.

nodes.label: Server-Computed Quote
nodes.rationale: Pricing, coupons and tax breakdown come from quote_subscription in the database, and begin_subscription_checkout recomputes them again before a payment record exists. The browser is never trusted with a total, and the summary panel renders only figures the server returned.

nodes.label: Permission-Not-Role Gating of Actions
nodes.rationale: Screens gate on permission constants, never on role strings. Both KOT boards require kot.view to render; the manager board's canAct flag is a separate kot.accept check. The Owner therefore gets a full but read-only board without any Owner-specific branch existing in the UI (PRD 5.2, PRD 9).

nodes.label: Kitchen Sees Accepted Work Only
nodes.rationale: The kitchen board queries KITCHEN_STATUSES while the manager board queries the wider ACTIVE_STATUSES. Accept/reject is a commercial decision the manager owns; showing the kitchen an unaccepted ticket would invite cooking food no one has agreed to sell. It also means the kitchen screen never carries prices or payment state.

nodes.label: Demo Panel Environment Gating
nodes.rationale: listDemoAccounts returns null unless SHOW_DEMO_ACCOUNTS is set, so the seeded credentials are never queried, never serialised to the client, and the panel is never rendered in a real storefront. The gate is on the server side of the boundary, not a CSS hide.

nodes.label: Lifted Credential State
nodes.rationale: Email and password live in SignInPanel and are passed down as value/onChange, so the demo panel fills the form by setting state directly. The alternative -- SignInForm syncing to a prop in an effect -- would keep a second copy in step. One owner, no copy.

nodes.label: Non-Enumerating Auth Error
nodes.rationale: Both sign-in surfaces collapse every credential failure into the identical sentence 'That email and password combination did not work.' Distinguishing 'no such account' from 'wrong password' would let an attacker enumerate which emails exist.

nodes.label: Confirm Destructive Actions
nodes.rationale: PRD 19. Pause and cancel each expand into a second-step form with an explicit confirm and an escape ('Never mind' / 'Keep my subscription'), and the cancel path states up front that deliveries already with the kitchen will still be prepared, so the customer is not surprised by food arriving after cancelling.

nodes.label: Colour Is Never the Only Indicator
nodes.rationale: PRD 19 accessibility rule. The revenue chart's legend pairs each swatch with the literal SX/SW/ZM code and its label, and every bar segment carries a <title> giving date, channel and amount, so the chart is readable without colour perception.
nodes.norm_label: colour is never the only indicator

nodes.label: Dependency-Free Last-Resort Boundary
nodes.rationale: global-error.tsx replaces the root layout when the shell itself fails, so it imports nothing -- no fonts, no design tokens, no UI primitives -- and hard-codes hex colours and system-ui inline. Anything it imported could be the thing that broke.

nodes.label: Server-Filtered Navigation
nodes.rationale: The admin nav receives an already permission-filtered sections array and only renders and highlights. Authorization stays on the server (requirePermission plus RLS); a hidden link is a courtesy, never the control.

nodes.label: PERMISSIONS.kotView
nodes.rationale: The permission that admits a user to either KOT board. Held by Owner, Manager and Kitchen alike, which is why all three can watch the same tickets.

nodes.label: PERMISSIONS.kotAccept
nodes.rationale: The permission that turns the manager board from a display into a console. Absent for the Owner, which is the entire mechanism behind the Owner's read-only board.

nodes.label: ingest_marketplace_order (RPC)
nodes.rationale: Idempotent on the provider's external order and event ids, so the route can hand it a replayed webhook without creating a duplicate KOT ticket.

nodes.label: record_integration_failure (RPC)
nodes.rationale: Called only in the catch path, scoped to one provider, so the circuit breaker it feeds is per-integration.

nodes.label: confirm_subscription_payment (RPC)
nodes.rationale: The single convergence point for the browser callback and the webhook. Idempotent, so a race between the two yields one activation, one credit grant, one invoice.

nodes.label: fail_subscription_payment (RPC)
nodes.rationale: Called with p_uncertain=false from the webhook, because a provider-reported failure is definitive in a way a dropped browser callback is not.

nodes.label: begin_subscription_checkout (RPC)
nodes.rationale: Named in the checkout page's comment as the point where the price is recomputed before a payment is created; the call itself lives in the payment step, not this file.

nodes.label: integration_events (table)
nodes.rationale: Audit trail for inbound marketplace traffic. Both rejected (signature_valid false, status failed) and verified-but-unhandled (status ignored) payloads are written here rather than discarded, so nothing arrives invisibly.

nodes.label: payment_events (table)
nodes.rationale: Carries the unique index on (provider, provider_event_id) that implements webhook deduplication. Rows are updated with processed_at, and with processing_error when no internal payment matches, so unmatched events queue for reconciliation.

nodes.label: customer_addresses (table)
nodes.rationale: Only one row per customer may be default, so saveAddress first clears is_default across the customer's addresses before inserting the new one as default.

nodes.label: BoardTicket / KOT board status sets
nodes.rationale: One ticket shape and two status sets (KITCHEN_STATUSES, ACTIVE_STATUSES) shared by both boards, so the difference between the kitchen and manager screens is a filter over the same data rather than two divergent models.

nodes.label: buttonClasses (single button visual definition)
nodes.rationale: One visual definition shared by Button (a real <button>, client-side so it can react to a pending form) and ButtonLink (a real <a>, server-safe). Keeping the classes in one module means the two renderings can never drift apart. The lg size exists because operational screens are read at arm's length on a tablet or kiosk.

nodes.label: Button
nodes.rationale: Reads useFormStatus so every server-action form gets a disabled state and spinner without each page wiring one up; most admin/account mutations are plain form posts and a slow save that looks like a dead button gets clicked twice (PRD 19 loading states; PRD 11 idempotency -- but not needing the idempotency is better still).

nodes.label: ConfirmButton (two-click destructive submit)
nodes.rationale: First click arms and turns the button danger-red so the second click is a decision rather than a repeat; a 4s timer and onBlur disarm it. No modal because these live in dense admin tables where a dialog per row is heavier than the action deserves, and the two-click pattern keeps the confirmation where the eye already is (PRD 19).

nodes.label: UI Primitives barrel
nodes.rationale: Single import surface: re-exports cx, Button, ConfirmButton and Spinner alongside the surface/feedback/form primitives, so feature components import one module rather than reaching into the design system file by file.

nodes.label: ButtonLink (navigation styled as a button)
nodes.rationale: A real <a>, not a <button> inside a <Link>: nesting interactive elements is invalid HTML, confuses screen readers about what one tab stop does, and breaks open-in-new-tab. Anything that GOES somewhere uses this; anything that DOES something uses Button.

nodes.label: SourceTag (KOT order-source marker)
nodes.rationale: Always renders the literal SW/ZM/SX prefix alongside the colour, because colour must never be the only source indicator (PRD 19) -- a colour-blind manager, or a washed-out kitchen screen, still reads the letters.

nodes.label: Stat (figure with caveat hint)
nodes.rationale: The hint slot carries the caveat: an estimate built on dummy cost assumptions should say so rather than looking like a fact (PRD 12).

nodes.label: CONTROL (shared form control classes)
nodes.rationale: Input, Select and Textarea all compose one CONTROL class string so the three controls share border, focus and disabled treatment by construction rather than by convention.

nodes.label: KitchenBoard (kitchen display)
nodes.rationale: Kanban columns with deliberately large type and no money anywhere -- built to be read across a counter (PRD 5.4, 9, 19). All three kitchen accounts share the physical display, so it names the signed-in one. The kitchen may start preparing but may not mark ready: the cook tells the manager verbally. That business rule is enforced in the database, and this screen simply does not offer a button the kitchen's role would be refused for.

nodes.label: ManagerBoard (KOT manager controller)
nodes.rationale: Accept, reject with reason, override ETA, mark ready after the kitchen says so verbally, record handoff (PRD 5.3, 9). Grouped by stage so decisions waiting on the manager sit at the top. A canAct=false role gets a read-only banner instead of hidden-but-clickable controls, and the signed-in name is always shown because the tablet is shared.

nodes.label: useTicketActions (KOT mutation hook)
nodes.rationale: Two behaviours matter: offline actions are refused up front because a button that appears to work offline falsely claims the change was persisted (PRD 11, 19); and the server's refusal -- illegal transition, or a role that may not make it -- is surfaced verbatim rather than leaving a silently unchanged board. A network failure mid-request is reported as genuinely unknown rather than guessed either way.

nodes.label: TicketItems (per-ticket line items)
nodes.rationale: Reads v_kot_ticket_items, which masks unit price and line total unless the reader holds orders.view_financial -- a Kitchen session receives no money at all rather than receiving it and being trusted not to render it (PRD 5.4, 17). Fetched per ticket rather than joined into the board query, because the board must stay fast under a realtime firehose and most tickets are never expanded.

nodes.label: ConnectionBadge (realtime state indicator)
nodes.rationale: A board that has quietly stopped updating is worse than one that says it has stopped, so reconnecting and offline are shown as prominently as live, with last-synced time and an explicit 'do not rely on it' when offline (PRD 11, 19).

nodes.label: kot.mark_ready permission
nodes.rationale: Held by the branch manager, not kitchen staff: the cook tells the manager verbally and the manager performs the step. The kitchen display never renders this action, and the DB transition trigger would refuse it anyway.

nodes.label: orders.view_financial permission
nodes.rationale: The gate that decides whether unit price and line total survive the v_kot_ticket_items view; a kitchen session simply never receives the numbers.

nodes.label: landingPathForRole
nodes.rationale: Typed as next Route so renaming any of these pages is a compile error rather than a staff member landing on a 404 after sign-in.

nodes.label: authorizeRequest (API-route guard)
nodes.rationale: Returns a 401/403-shaped result instead of redirecting, because an API route answering a fetch must produce a status the client hook can turn into a message, not an HTML redirect.

nodes.label: listDemoAccounts
nodes.rationale: Reads auth_profiles rather than hardcoding emails so a staff account added through /admin/employees shows up automatically and the list cannot drift from the database it claims to describe. Uses the service role because an anonymous visitor cannot read auth_profiles -- which is correct, and is why the function is flag-gated before it runs. A panel that cannot load is simply absent: it is a convenience and must never be why nobody can reach the sign-in form.

nodes.label: explainAbsence (one-shot server log)
nodes.rationale: Logs once per process why the panel is missing: absence is otherwise indistinguishable from a broken build, and the vars live in gitignored .env.local which never travels with a push. Once per process so it explains itself on a cold start without narrating every request.

nodes.label: ROLE_NOTES / ROLE_LABELS / ROLE_ORDER
nodes.rationale: Ordered most-privileged first so the sign-in list reads top-down like the org chart; the notes restate each role's operational boundary (owner watches the KOT but cannot touch it, kitchen sees no money).

nodes.label: draftSchema (checkout draft cookie)
nodes.rationale: Lives in an httpOnly cookie rather than the database because the customer may not have an account yet -- account creation happens late in checkout (PRD 6). Nothing in it is trusted: price is recomputed by quote_subscription, plan/window pairing and meal selections are re-validated by begin_subscription_checkout, and the address is checked to belong to the signed-in customer. A tampered cookie can at worst select a plan the customer could have chosen anyway.

nodes.label: draft idempotencyKey
nodes.rationale: Generated once when the configuration is saved and reused for every retry -- that is what makes a double-submit, a browser crash mid-payment or a refresh of the checkout page produce one subscription rather than several (PRD 7, PRD 11).

nodes.label: Checkout client privilege split
nodes.rationale: serverClient() (the user's own token) runs everything the customer is doing so RLS and ownership guards apply to them specifically; adminClient() runs only the two things a browser must never do -- confirming a payment and failing one -- plus recording the gateway order id, since payments has no client write policy. Reaching for the admin client to 'simplify' the customer-facing half would quietly delete the protection this flow exists to provide.

nodes.label: ConfirmOutcome (active | failed | needs_reconciliation)
nodes.rationale: Three outcomes rather than two: an unverifiable payment is neither success nor plain failure, so it is reported as needs_reconciliation with the explicit statement that money may have moved and no subscription exists yet.

nodes.label: PaymentStep (address, provider, pay)
nodes.rationale: All three outcomes are shown honestly (PRD 8, 19). Offline is refused before anything starts so a dead browser never looks mid-payment; a drop before begin is stated as safely retryable; a drop mid-confirmation says the outcome is genuinely unknown and tells the customer not to pay again. The retry copy explains that retrying reuses the same checkout rather than creating a second subscription.

nodes.label: completeSandbox (test gateway outcome)
nodes.rationale: The sandbox asks the operator to pick success / decline / time out; each outcome is signed on the server and verified through the same path a real provider uses, so the uncertain branch is exercisable end to end.

nodes.label: PlanConfigurator
nodes.rationale: Deliberately does no pricing arithmetic of its own -- it shows the plan price and lets the server produce the real quote at checkout, because a total computed here would be a second source of truth and the one the customer remembers. Unavailable meals are shown disabled with their reason instead of being dropped from the grid.

nodes.label: ProfileStep
nodes.rationale: Collects the PRD 6 required profile data (full name, mobile; address next). Marketing consent is asked separately and defaults to off -- it is not bundled into 'create my account'.

nodes.label: toCard (row to ProductCard mapper)
nodes.rationale: Picks the primary image (falling back to the first) and falls back to the product name for alt text, so every card renders accessibly regardless of how the images were curated.

nodes.label: loadRatings (v_product_ratings lookup)
nodes.rationale: Ratings are looked up separately rather than embedded because they come from a view; callers that do not care (a plan's meal list, a collection tile) pass nothing and get a card with no rating. Only published reviews are counted -- the view excludes everything else.

nodes.label: listMenu
nodes.rationale: Unavailable products are still returned: the menu shows them grayscale with a badge rather than hiding them (PRD 6, PRD 19).

nodes.label: publicSettings / listPublicOffers
nodes.rationale: Sensitive settings keys and non-public coupons are filtered by RLS, so a storefront call cannot reach one even by asking for it by key.

nodes.label: ProductTile
nodes.rationale: An unavailable product renders grayscale with an explicit badge and reason and is not selectable (PRD 6, 19) -- shown rather than hidden, so a customer learns what the kitchen normally makes and why it is off today.

nodes.label: fail / done (server-action redirect feedback)
nodes.rationale: A server action cannot return a value to a server-rendered page, so the outcome travels back in the query string and the page renders it. A create form that silently does nothing when the database rejects it is how an Owner ends up believing a plan exists when it does not. The typed-Route cast is on the assembled URL only -- path itself is a literal at every call site.

nodes.label: readable (Postgres error translator)
nodes.rationale: Postgres errors are precise but not phrased for a person: 23505 becomes a duplicate-code message, 23503 tells the Owner to hide the record instead of deleting it, 42501 becomes a permission sentence.

nodes.label: FormData readers (str/num/list)
nodes.rationale: A server action receives everything as a string, so these turn it back into the shape each column expects. The load-bearing distinction is a cleared field versus a zero one: writing '' into a nullable numeric column is an error rather than a null, and writing 0 where the Owner meant 'no override' silently changes policy.

nodes.label: nullableBool (tri-state)
nodes.rationale: A plan-level rule left blank means 'use the global setting', which is a genuinely different answer from false -- the default has to keep living in exactly one place (PRD 20). Also why bool() defaults to false: an unchecked checkbox is absent from FormData entirely.

nodes.label: slugify / codify
nodes.rationale: Derives a URL-safe slug (or an uppercase code) so create forms do not make the Owner invent one; slugs stay editable afterwards -- a starting point, not a rule.

nodes.label: Refuse offline mutations up front
nodes.rationale: navigator.onLine is checked before any mutating fetch, in both the KOT hook and the payment step. A button that appears to work while offline would falsely claim the change was persisted; the UI says so instead of letting the request time out (PRD 11, 19).

nodes.label: Report unknown outcomes as unknown
nodes.rationale: When a request drops mid-flight the result is genuinely unknown, so neither success nor failure is guessed: KOT says 'check the ticket before trying again', checkout says money may have moved, nothing is active yet, do not pay again, and reconciliation will settle it.

nodes.label: Two-click destructive confirmation
nodes.rationale: Destructive actions must survive a stray click without a modal per table row: arm-then-confirm keeps the confirmation where the eye already is, auto-disarms after 4 seconds and on blur. Rejection on the manager board applies the same principle in a heavier form, requiring an explicit reason as well as a second click.

nodes.label: No money on kitchen screens
nodes.rationale: The kitchen display renders no monetary value anywhere, and the data layer enforces it: v_kot_ticket_items masks unit price and line total unless the reader holds orders.view_financial, so a kitchen session receives no money at all rather than receiving it and being trusted not to render it (PRD 5.4, 17). The manager board, whose role does hold it, renders money() freely.

nodes.label: A hidden button is not a security boundary
nodes.rationale: The session permission Set decides only what the UI renders. Every mutation is re-authorized server-side by RLS or by the KOT transition trigger, so an operator who forges a request gets the same refusal the screen implied -- and the client surfaces that refusal verbatim.
nodes.norm_label: a hidden button is not a security boundary

nodes.label: Role-to-permission mapping is data, not code
nodes.rationale: PERMISSIONS holds only the codes so TypeScript can catch a typo in a guard; which role holds which permission lives in role_permissions and is queried at session load. The same instinct drives listDemoAccounts reading auth_profiles instead of hardcoding a list of emails.
nodes.norm_label: role-to-permission mapping is data, not code

nodes.label: Checkout idempotency by draft key
nodes.rationale: One key is minted when the plan configuration is saved and carried in the cookie through every retry, so begin_subscription_checkout replays instead of creating a second subscription; the service then reuses any existing gateway order id for that payment, so a replay does not open a second gateway order either. The UI states this to the customer on the failure screen.

nodes.label: Server is the only source of price
nodes.rationale: The configurator shows the plan price and defers taxes, offers and totals to the server quote. A total computed in the browser would be a second source of truth and the one the customer remembers if the two disagree.
nodes.norm_label: server is the only source of price

nodes.label: Show unavailable, do not hide it
nodes.rationale: listMenu deliberately returns unavailable products so the storefront can render them grayscale with a reason (PRD 6, 19): hiding them teaches the customer nothing, while showing them communicates what the kitchen normally makes and why it is off today. The plan configurator repeats the pattern with disabled selection tiles.
nodes.norm_label: show unavailable, do not hide it

nodes.label: Colour is never the only signal
nodes.rationale: SourceTag prints the literal SW/ZM/SX code beside its colour, badges carry text, and the overdue state adds a border plus a label rather than only turning red -- for colour-blind operators and washed-out kitchen screens alike (PRD 19).
nodes.norm_label: colour is never the only signal

nodes.label: RLS decides what the read models return
nodes.rationale: Every storefront read runs through the user's (or anonymous) client, so an unpublished product, a non-public coupon or a sensitive settings key is invisible without this file knowing any publication rule. The checkout service follows the same split, reserving the admin client for payment confirmation only.
nodes.norm_label: rls decides what the read models return

nodes.label: serverEnv() validated environment
nodes.rationale: Zod-parses process.env once and caches it, throwing a readable list of every missing variable at first use rather than letting Supabase fail later with an opaque 500. Business rules (fees, taxes, grace periods, delivery windows) are deliberately kept OUT of the environment and stored as database rows so they can change without a deploy; only credentials and deployment wiring live here.

nodes.label: blankAsUndefined preprocessor
nodes.rationale: An unset key in a .env file is an empty string, not undefined. Coercing '' to undefined is what lets .env.example ship with every optional key present but blank; otherwise a blank SWIGGY_API_BASE_URL fails z.string().url() and takes the whole app down at boot.

nodes.label: resolveSecret(ref) indirection
nodes.rationale: integration_accounts stores the NAME of an env var, never the secret itself. Only this function dereferences it, and it whitelists /^[A-Z0-9_]+$/ so a compromised database row cannot be used to read arbitrary process state.

nodes.label: Secrets live in the environment only
nodes.rationale: PRD 17/20: secrets never in the database and never in a client bundle. The database records which variable to look up; env.ts is the single module that resolves it. Corollary: business rules are data (DB rows), credentials are configuration (env) -- the two are deliberately not mixed.
nodes.norm_label: secrets live in the environment only

nodes.label: SHOW_DEMO_ACCOUNTS explicit switch
nodes.rationale: A single explicit flag rather than a NODE_ENV check, because the thing being reviewed is usually a deployed preview where NODE_ENV is always 'production'. Unset, the demo panel stops existing -- the sign-in page never even queries for it.

nodes.label: BUSINESS_TIMEZONE formatters (Asia/Kolkata)
nodes.rationale: The database computes the business day in Asia/Kolkata (PRD 10); every formatter pins timeZone to the same zone so a ticket created at 00:30 IST never renders under the previous day.

nodes.label: money() / moneyExact()
nodes.rationale: Accepts the strings Postgres returns for `numeric` directly, because pushing Number() to the call site is where rounding bugs start. Nulls and NaN render as an em dash rather than 'NaN' or '0'.

nodes.label: SOURCE_LABELS / KOT_STATUS_LABELS
nodes.rationale: SX/SW/ZM prefixes are always shown as text: colour is never the only cue distinguishing a website order from a Swiggy or Zomato one.

nodes.label: isAuthorisedJob() cron guard
nodes.rationale: Scheduled jobs run with the service role and can release deliveries into the kitchen, so they are gated by a shared secret (CRON_SECRET) rather than a user session -- there is no human actor to authenticate. Comparison is timingSafeEqual after an explicit length check, because a timing oracle on this header would recover the secret over many requests.

nodes.label: MarketplaceAdapter interface
nodes.rationale: PRD 16 contract. isLive is true only when a base URL and credential actually exist, so the Owner's integration screen can never imply a connection the system does not have.

nodes.label: CapabilityState (integrated | mocked | blocked)
nodes.rationale: Capabilities are marked 'blocked' rather than guessed because Swiggy/Zomato grant partner API access per merchant under contract and no such contract or documentation exists here. 'blocked' returns an explicit refusal; inventing a plausible endpoint URL would silently drop real orders.

nodes.label: IncomingOrder envelope
nodes.rationale: Normalised shape both marketplaces are mapped onto, carrying `raw` so the original payload survives for reconciliation and dispute.

nodes.label: No endpoint is ever invented
nodes.rationale: The governing constraint of the whole marketplace module. Every capability carries an explicit recorded state, an adapter method checks that state before acting, and the same states are surfaced in the Owner UI so the interface and the code agree about what is real.

nodes.label: PartnerMarketplaceAdapter
nodes.rationale: One class serves both Swiggy and Zomato because there are no documented differences to encode -- they differ only by AdapterConfig (baseUrlEnv/apiKeyEnv/webhookSecretEnv). When a real partner contract arrives, the provider-specific request shapes become a subclass and the capability register moves from 'blocked' to 'integrated' at the same time.

nodes.label: capabilityState() lookup
nodes.rationale: Reads integration_capabilities via the service-role client and defaults an unknown/missing row to 'blocked'. Fail-closed: a capability nobody has explicitly enabled is not attempted.

nodes.label: attempt() capability gate + circuit breaker
nodes.rationale: Every outbound call passes through here. 'blocked' returns {ok:false} with a reason and sends nothing; 'integrated' calls live but first re-checks isLive so a mislabelled row cannot produce a fetch against `undefined`; anything else runs the mock transport and tags the result via:'mock'. Success and failure are recorded through record_integration_success / record_integration_failure RPCs keyed on p_provider, so the breaker state is per-provider in the database -- a Swiggy outage trips Swiggy's circuit only and leaves Zomato and the website untouched (PRD 16).

nodes.label: PartnerMarketplaceAdapter.verifyWebhook()
nodes.rationale: Plain HMAC-SHA256 hex of the raw body, read from x-webhook-signature or x-{provider}-signature, compared with an explicit length check plus timingSafeEqual. Missing secret or missing header is a rejection, not a pass-through: until a real integration is confirmed an unsigned payload is refused rather than trusted.

nodes.label: interpretPayload() best-effort mapper
nodes.rationale: Reads the common envelope shapes (order|data|body, order_id|id, event|type) and returns kind:'other' with a reason rather than mangling a payload it does not recognise. Runs only AFTER the signature check, so unrecognised-but-authentic traffic is surfaced instead of silently coerced.

nodes.label: marketplaceAdapter() provider registry
nodes.rationale: Per-provider Map cache. Each provider is constructed independently, so constructing or failing one has no effect on the other -- the process-level half of the isolation that keeps a Swiggy outage from stopping Zomato orders.

nodes.label: providerForSource(source)
nodes.rationale: Maps the KOT ticket source prefix (SW/ZM) onto the owning marketplace provider, returning null for SX (website) so an internal order never triggers an outbound partner call.

nodes.label: NotificationTransport interface
nodes.rationale: SendResult.retryable is tri-state on purpose: `false` marks a permanent failure (a bad number) that must go straight to dead_letter instead of burning the retry budget.

nodes.label: ConsoleTransport
nodes.rationale: The default when NOTIFICATION_PROVIDER is unset. It logs what would have been sent and reports sent:true -- a working, honest default rather than a stub that pretends to deliver, chosen because the provider and notification matrix are decided later (PRD 15).

nodes.label: TwilioTransport
nodes.rationale: Missing credentials return retryable:false rather than throwing, so a misconfiguration dead-letters instead of looping. Twilio HTTP status maps to retryability: >=500 is retryable, a 4xx means the request itself is wrong and retrying will not fix it.

nodes.label: renderTemplate()
nodes.rationale: An unknown {{placeholder}} is left visible rather than blanked, so a broken template is obvious in testing instead of shipping a message with a hole in it.

nodes.label: Notification failure never breaks an order
nodes.rationale: PRD 15. The outbox pattern decouples the delivery attempt from the transaction that produced it: if WhatsApp is down, subscriptions still activate and tickets still reach the kitchen.
nodes.norm_label: notification failure never breaks an order

nodes.label: PaymentAdapter interface
nodes.rationale: PRD 8/20. Two rules bind every implementation: (1) verification happens on the server via a cryptographic signature and never trusts a browser-reported status; (2) nothing in an adapter mutates application state -- it returns a verdict, and confirm_subscription_payment is what actually activates anything. verifyWebhook takes the RAW body because parsing first would break the signature.

nodes.label: VerificationResult.uncertain
nodes.rationale: A dedicated third outcome between verified and failed: money may have moved but the outcome is not confirmable. It routes to reconciliation rather than being guessed either way (PRD 8). WebhookEvent.eventId exists so uniqueness on it makes replays safe.

nodes.label: PaymentProviderError
nodes.rationale: Carries the provider id so a failure can be attributed to one gateway rather than reading as a generic checkout error.

nodes.label: paymentAdapter() factory
nodes.rationale: Cached per process because constructing an adapter reads the environment and none hold per-request state. 'cod' throws immediately: cash on delivery exists in the data model but is paused (PRD 3/8), and enabling it needs a settings change AND a real adapter -- never a silent fallthrough that marks an order paid because nobody objected. An adapter whose isConfigured is false throws at resolution rather than being handed to a checkout that would fail at the gateway.

nodes.label: availablePaymentProviders()
nodes.rationale: The list a customer may actually choose from, flagged with isSandbox so the test gateway is always labelled as moving no real money.

nodes.label: RazorpayAdapter
nodes.rationale: Amounts cross this boundary in paise (x100 out, /100 back); nothing outside the file needs to know that, so the rest of the system stays in rupees. The checkout object it returns contains the publishable key_id only -- the secret never leaves the server. Refunds pass X-Razorpay-Idempotency so a retried refund does not double-pay.

nodes.label: Razorpay verifyCallback (order|payment HMAC)
nodes.rationale: Razorpay signs `${order_id}|${payment_id}` with the key secret; the server recomputes it. The browser's claim of success is never trusted -- only the recomputed HMAC decides.

nodes.label: Razorpay synthetic eventId dedupe key
nodes.rationale: Razorpay does not send a dedicated event id header on all plans, so `${event}:${payment.id}` is synthesised as the stable dedupe key. Without it, webhook replay protection would have nothing unique to key on.

nodes.label: signaturesMatch() constant-time compare
nodes.rationale: timingSafeEqual throws on differing lengths, so the helper length-checks first and returns false -- tolerating differing lengths without leaking them through an exception or a timing difference.

nodes.label: CashfreeAdapter
nodes.rationale: Absorbs two differences from Razorpay so the checkout code is identical for either provider: Cashfree works in rupees rather than paise, and returns a payment_session_id the browser SDK consumes instead of an order id. Base URL switches on CASHFREE_ENVIRONMENT; webhook secret falls back to CASHFREE_SECRET_KEY. Refund idempotency is achieved by sending the idempotencyKey as refund_id, which Cashfree dedupes on.

nodes.label: Cashfree verifyCallback (server re-query)
nodes.rationale: Cashfree's browser handshake carries no signature of its own, so verification cannot be cryptographic here. Instead the server asks Cashfree directly for the order's payments and treats the browser purely as a hint that something happened. A non-OK response returns uncertain:true rather than a verdict, and a PENDING payment is also uncertain -- both route to reconciliation instead of guessing.

nodes.label: Cashfree verifyWebhook (timestamp+body, base64)
nodes.rationale: Cashfree signs timestamp + rawBody and sends the digest base64-encoded in x-webhook-signature -- differing from Razorpay in both the signed material (the timestamp prefix binds the signature to a moment) and the encoding. Both headers are mandatory; either missing is a rejection.

nodes.label: SandboxAdapter (test gateway)
nodes.rationale: Exists to make the PRD's end-to-end flow demonstrable before a merchant account exists, without being a shortcut around the payment invariant: it signs `${orderId}|${paymentId}` with HMAC-SHA256 exactly as Razorpay does and recomputes it on verify, so a forged or altered callback fails and confirm_subscription_payment refuses to activate a subscription. It refuses to construct at all in production. The signing key is CRON_SECRET, an already-existing server-only shared secret a browser cannot mint a signature with.

nodes.label: Sandbox refuses to construct in production
nodes.rationale: Throws from the constructor when ENABLE_SANDBOX_PAYMENTS==='true' and NODE_ENV==='production' rather than quietly setting enabled=false. Loud, not silent: leaving a fake gateway on in production would be a real incident, so the failure must be impossible to miss. Defence in depth with configuredPaymentProviders(), which already refuses to offer sandbox in production.
nodes.norm_label: sandbox refuses to construct in production

nodes.label: signOutcome() server-side outcome signing
nodes.rationale: Called by the server-side sandbox endpoint when a tester chooses succeed or fail -- never by the browser, which has no access to the signing key. This is what keeps the sandbox honest: the browser receives identifiers only and must ask the server to sign.

nodes.label: A correctly signed failure is still a failure
nodes.rationale: verifyCallback checks the signature first, then reads `outcome`: a valid signature over outcome:'failed' returns verified:false, and outcome:'uncertain' returns uncertain:true. Verification proves the message is authentic, not that the payment succeeded -- conflating the two is the classic signature-verification bug this guards against.
nodes.norm_label: a correctly signed failure is still a failure

nodes.label: ACTIVE_STATUSES / KITCHEN_STATUSES
nodes.rationale: Split into a non-'use client' module on purpose: a value exported from a client module and imported by a Server Component arrives as a client reference rather than the value, so ACTIVE_STATUSES would silently become a function and `new Set(...)` would throw at request time. KITCHEN_STATUSES is narrower -- the kitchen display shows accepted work onward, never unaccepted tickets.

nodes.label: useKotBoard() live KOT hook
nodes.rationale: PRD 11. Realtime is the mechanism, not a garnish on polling -- there is no interval anywhere in the hook. Tickets are held in a Map keyed by id so writes are idempotent, and sorted by priority+urgency_score with created_at as tiebreak (marketplace orders outrank scheduled deliveries; an approaching deadline escalates anything, PRD 9). Connection state is surfaced so nobody trusts a stale board, and actions are refused while offline rather than appearing to succeed.

nodes.label: refetchOne() -- event as signal, not data
nodes.rationale: The postgres_changes payload is used ONLY for its row id; the row is then re-read from v_kot_tickets. Two reasons: the server stays authoritative so the view's money-masking still applies, and duplicate or out-of-order events become harmless -- a replayed event just re-reads the same row and a late event cannot resurrect stale values. A row that is gone, or whose status left ACTIVE_STATUSES, is deleted from the Map, so completion removes the card by the same path as any other change.
nodes.norm_label: refetchone() -- event as signal, not data

nodes.label: resync() full resynchronisation
nodes.rationale: Recovery, not polling. Triggered on three edges: a SUBSCRIBED status when hasConnectedRef is already true (a genuine reconnect, not the first connect -- the server already rendered the board), the window 'online' event, and visibilitychange to visible. The last exists because a backgrounded tab can have its socket dropped without any error ever firing, so returning to the tab must not show a silently stale board.

nodes.label: ConnectionState (connecting|live|reconnecting|offline)
nodes.rationale: CHANNEL_ERROR and TIMED_OUT map to 'reconnecting'; CLOSED maps to 'reconnecting' unless already 'offline', so the browser's own offline signal (which arrives before the socket times out) is not overwritten by a slower socket event.

nodes.label: adminClient() service-role client
nodes.rationale: Bypasses RLS, so it is reserved for work with no authenticated user behind it that the database must nonetheless trust: verifying a payment webhook, ingesting a marketplace order, releasing due deliveries, reconciliation. Every route reaching for it performs its own authorization check first. Where there IS a user, serverClient() must be used instead so RLS, the transition permission checks and the audit trail resolve to that person -- reaching for the service role to 'just make it work' would discard exactly the protections the system is built on. persistSession/autoRefreshToken are off because there is no session to keep.

nodes.label: auditSystemEvent()
nodes.rationale: Webhooks and scheduled jobs genuinely have no human actor, so the entry is attributed to the system with a `context` naming the subsystem -- more truthful than borrowing a user's identity for a machine's action. It logs and swallows RPC errors: losing real completed work to a logging problem is the worse failure. The database's app.actor_id session setting is deliberately not used here because PostgREST pools connections and a session-level setting would leak into an unrelated request.

nodes.label: browserClient() anon browser client
nodes.rationale: Holds the anon key only. Realtime change events are filtered by the same RLS policies that govern reads, so a Kitchen session receives ticket changes and nothing else (PRD 11) -- authorisation for the live board is enforced in the database, not in the hook.

nodes.label: serverClient() request-scoped user client
nodes.rationale: Carries the signed-in user's cookies, so every query is RLS-filtered as that user and every RPC sees them as auth.uid() -- which is how KOT transition checks, subscription ownership guards and the audit trail resolve to a real person without the application passing an identity around. setAll swallows its error because Server Components cannot set cookies; the middleware refreshes the session instead.

nodes.label: createTestDb() PGlite harness
nodes.rationale: Applies the shim then the real migration set in filename order against PGlite (Postgres in WASM), so tests exercise the actual constraints, triggers, RLS policies and RPCs rather than a mock. Migration failures are re-thrown naming the file, so a broken migration is diagnosable rather than surfacing as a mystery query error later.

nodes.label: actingAs() principal switch
nodes.rationale: Wraps each block in a transaction with SET LOCAL role and request.jwt.claims so the principal never leaks into the next test, and so RLS is evaluated against a genuinely non-superuser role -- run as superuser, every policy would be bypassed and the tests would prove nothing. This is the single mechanism that makes every negative authorisation test in the suite meaningful.

nodes.label: supabase-shim.sql
nodes.rationale: Recreates the subset of Supabase that the schema depends on (auth schema, auth.users, auth.uid(), the anon/authenticated/service_role roles) because PGlite is a bare Postgres. It mirrors GoTrue's real nullability quirks deliberately -- token columns default to '' not NULL, and the timestamp columns have NO default -- so a seed that omits them fails in the harness rather than producing 'Database error querying schema' on every login in production. Never applied to a real environment; it lives under tests/.

nodes.label: Fixed seed identifiers
nodes.rationale: Named constants for the UUIDs in supabase/seed.sql so assertions read as intent (SANA, PRODUCT_BIRYANI) rather than as hex. Couples the test suite to the seed file: changing a seeded id must change this file.

nodes.label: Test: verified-purchase badge is derived, not claimed
nodes.rationale: Proves the database refuses a customer's self-asserted is_verified_purchase when nothing was delivered to them, grants it once a delivery of that dish is fulfilled, and leaves a trusted importer's record alone. The invariant: trust flags are computed from fulfilment facts, never accepted from the client.
nodes.norm_label: test: verified-purchase badge is derived, not claimed

nodes.label: Test: review moderation authority and audit
nodes.rationale: Proves a pending review is invisible to the public, a moderator can publish it and the decision records who and why, a customer cannot moderate, a branch manager cannot either (permission-based, not seniority-based), and a no-op decision records nothing -- so the audit trail contains decisions rather than clicks.
nodes.norm_label: test: review moderation authority and audit

nodes.label: Test: staff roles, addresses, refund cases
nodes.rationale: Proves privilege escalation is blocked at the database (a customer cannot change anyone's role, least of all their own), one customer cannot write an address onto another's account, a customer may raise and withdraw only their own refund case, a decided case cannot be withdrawn, and no customer decides their own case. All enforced by RLS, so a route bug cannot bypass it.
nodes.norm_label: test: staff roles, addresses, refund cases

nodes.label: Test: coupons are validated server-side
nodes.rationale: Exercises validate_coupon() directly: first-subscription eligibility, refusal after an activation or a prior redemption, percentage caps, minimum order amounts, expiry, and an unknown code rejected without throwing. Also proves redemption happens exactly once per subscription -- the discount rules are a database function, not client arithmetic.

nodes.label: Test: the quote is computed server-side
nodes.rationale: Proves CGST/SGST are split and total correctly, a coupon that did not apply reports WHY instead of being silently dropped, an unpublished plan cannot be quoted, and changing the tax rate row changes the total with no code change.
nodes.norm_label: test: the quote is computed server-side

nodes.label: Test: configuration is data, not constants
nodes.rationale: Proves the delivery fee (including the free-above threshold) and the KOT release lead time come from rows and change without touching code, that a missing required setting fails loudly rather than defaulting to zero, that rules awaiting owner sign-off are marked provisional, and that COD is present in the model but switched off. This is the test-side counterpart of env.ts deliberately holding no business rules.
nodes.norm_label: test: configuration is data, not constants

nodes.label: Test: realtime is wired for the operational tables
nodes.rationale: Asserts kot_tickets, kot_status_events and subscription_deliveries are in the supabase_realtime publication, that replica identity is FULL ('f') on kot_tickets/orders/subscription_deliveries, and that exactly one SELECT policy governs kot_tickets -- so the same RLS policy that gates reads gates which change events reach a kitchen client. Without the publication rows the KOT board would receive nothing and its no-polling design would fail silently.
nodes.norm_label: test: realtime is wired for the operational tables

nodes.label: Role: Customer
nodes.rationale: Indian metro, mobile-first, in a buying mood — the storefront may lean warm and appetising, but checkout is a task.

nodes.label: Role: Branch Manager
nodes.rationale: Runs the kitchen floor from a tablet, time-pressed mid-rush; accepts/rejects tickets, overrides ETAs, marks ready and hands off. Holds no pricing, payment, profit or analytics permission.

nodes.label: Role: Kitchen Staff
nodes.rationale: Three accounts on one shared physical wall display, read at arm's length under bad lighting. Because the display is shared and public, staff must never see money — only kot.view and kot.start_prep.

nodes.label: Role: Owner
nodes.rationale: Business oversight from a laptop: analytics, catalog, plans, coupons, customers, reviews, settings, audit. The Owner watches the kitchen and cannot touch it, so the KOT is read-only.

nodes.label: Role: Developer Admin
nodes.rationale: Maximum Phase 1 access for integrations and configuration; holds every permission — but still cannot rewrite the append-only audit log.

nodes.label: Unified KOT Across Three Channels
nodes.rationale: One kitchen prepares food for Website (SX), Swiggy (SW) and Zomato (ZM), so one board must show all three rather than three separate screens.

nodes.label: Brand Personality: Warm, Trustworthy, Operational
nodes.rationale: The storefront reads as food, not SaaS; the operations surface reads as equipment. Confidence comes from things visibly working — honest states, honest numbers, caveats on estimates.

nodes.label: Anti-references (What This Must Not Look Like)
nodes.rationale: No generic SaaS gradient dashboard, no Swiggy/Zomato clone styling, nothing that hides state, no decoration on KOT screens — kitchen screens are instruments, not marketing.
nodes.norm_label: anti-references (what this must not look like)

nodes.label: Principle: The Database Is the Truth
nodes.rationale: The UI never claims more than it knows. Offline actions never fake persistence; estimates built on dummy costs say so.
nodes.norm_label: principle: the database is the truth

nodes.label: Principle: Color Is Never the Only Signal
nodes.rationale: Color-blind safety by construction: every source badge carries its literal prefix (SW/ZM/SX) and every state has a text label.
nodes.norm_label: principle: color is never the only signal

nodes.label: Principle: Glanceable Under Rush
nodes.rationale: Operational screens optimise for arm's-length reading: big type, high contrast, Kanban columns, one obvious action per ticket state.

nodes.label: Principle: Role-Shaped Interfaces
nodes.rationale: Kitchen sees no money, Owner's KOT has no buttons, Manager has no pricing. The UI enforces what RLS already guarantees — the UI is the second line, never the only one.

nodes.label: Principle: Confirm Destruction, Forgive Everything Else
nodes.rationale: Reject requires confirmation; ordinary actions are fast and idempotent, because a double tap under rush must not surface a failure.
nodes.norm_label: principle: confirm destruction, forgive everything else

nodes.label: Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA Intent
nodes.rationale: 4.5:1 body contrast on light and ops-dark, global :focus-visible rings, 44px touch targets on operational buttons, prefers-reduced-motion honored, storefront responsive to 375px.

nodes.label: Postgres Is the Authority
nodes.rationale: Business rules, permissions, the KOT state machine and every fee, tax and limit are rows, not constants — so the Owner retunes the business without a deploy. The application layer is a thin, typed shell over that.

nodes.label: Operational Writes Only Through SECURITY DEFINER Functions
nodes.rationale: Orders, payments, subscriptions and tickets have no client write policy at all; writes happen only through functions that validate state, permission and idempotency first, so a compromised browser token cannot forge state.
nodes.norm_label: operational writes only through security definer functions

nodes.label: Configuration as Rows (business_settings)
nodes.rationale: Raising kot.release_lead_time_minutes from the Owner UI released deliveries with no code change or redeploy. Missing settings fail loudly rather than defaulting silently.

nodes.label: Provisional Settings Awaiting Owner Validation
nodes.rationale: Delivery fee, pause limits, KOT lead time, prep estimates, GST split and marketplace commission assumptions are flagged is_provisional and visible as such, so an unvalidated number is never mistaken for a decided one.

nodes.label: Invariant: No Unverified Payment Creates an Order or KOT
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: Enforced by the subscriptions_require_verified_payment and kot_tickets_require_confirmed_order triggers, so the database holds even if application code slips.
nodes.norm_label: invariant: no unverified payment creates an order or kot

nodes.label: Invariant: Payment Verified Server-Side, Never From the Browser
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: confirm_subscription_payment refuses unless the adapter verified a signature; a browser token has no path to confirm its own payment.
nodes.norm_label: invariant: payment verified server-side, never from the browser

nodes.label: Invariant: Financial Operations Are Idempotent
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: Unique keys on payments.idempotency_key, (subscription_id, idempotency_key) on the ledger and (source, external_order_id) on orders, because gateways and marketplaces retry and a retry must never charge or cook twice.

nodes.label: Invariant: The Owner's KOT Is Read-Only
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: role_permissions grants the Owner kot.view and no transition permission; the UI renders 'Read-only view' and the API refuses the transition anyway.
nodes.norm_label: invariant: the owner's kot is read-only

nodes.label: Invariant: Kitchen Staff Get No Financial Data
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: Money columns are masked in v_kot_tickets / v_kot_ticket_items and kitchen holds no orders.view — the board is a shared public display, so masking happens in the view rather than the component.
nodes.norm_label: invariant: kitchen staff get no financial data

nodes.label: Invariant: One Marketplace Failing Cannot Stop Another
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: A per-provider circuit breaker on integration_accounts keeps a Swiggy outage from halting Zomato ingestion.
nodes.norm_label: invariant: one marketplace failing cannot stop another

nodes.label: Invariant: No Fabricated Marketplace Endpoints
nodes.rationale: Swiggy and Zomato grant partner API access per merchant under contract; this repo has none, so integration_capabilities gates every outbound call and 'blocked' refuses instead of guessing a URL.

nodes.label: Invariant: History Is Preserved
nodes.source_location: The invariants, and where they are enforced
nodes.rationale: Append-only triggers on audit_logs and the credit ledger plus snapshotted order lines: a corrected ledger is a compensating entry, never an edit.

nodes.label: Front-end Rule: Navigate Is an Anchor, Act Is a Button
nodes.rationale: A <button> inside a <Link> is invalid HTML and breaks open-in-new-tab, so ButtonLink renders a real <a> while Button acts.
nodes.norm_label: front-end rule: navigate is an anchor, act is a button

nodes.label: Front-end Rule: A Saving Form Says So
nodes.rationale: Button reads useFormStatus so every server-action submit disables itself and shows a spinner automatically — enforced by a shared component rather than by discipline.
nodes.norm_label: front-end rule: a saving form says so

nodes.label: Front-end Rule: A Destructive Action Needs Two Clicks
nodes.rationale: ConfirmButton arms on the first click, submits on the second and disarms after 4s (PRD 19).
nodes.norm_label: front-end rule: a destructive action needs two clicks

nodes.label: Front-end Rule: A Refused Write Is Reported, Never Swallowed
nodes.rationale: fail()/done() plus <ActionFeedback>, because a save that silently does nothing is how an Owner comes to believe a setting changed when it did not.
nodes.norm_label: front-end rule: a refused write is reported, never swallowed

nodes.label: Tests Run the Real Migrations on PGlite
nodes.rationale: 116 tests run Postgres compiled to WebAssembly so constraints, triggers, RLS policies and RPCs are exercised as themselves, with no Docker daemon and no mocking of the database.
nodes.norm_label: tests run the real migrations on pglite

nodes.label: Tests Act as Genuine Non-Superuser Roles
nodes.rationale: As superuser every policy would be bypassed and the suite would prove nothing, so each test runs as anon, authenticated or service_role.
nodes.norm_label: tests act as genuine non-superuser roles

nodes.label: Seed Data Built Through Real Workflows
nodes.rationale: The seed does not insert fake rows into orders or kot_tickets; it buys subscriptions, releases deliveries and ingests marketplace orders through the same functions the app calls, then asserts the PRD invariants so a regression fails the seed rather than producing quietly wrong data.
nodes.norm_label: seed data built through real workflows

nodes.label: The Sandbox Gateway Is Not a Bypass
nodes.rationale: It signs its callback with HMAC-SHA256 verified through the same path a real provider uses, and refuses to construct when NODE_ENV=production — a fake gateway must never be reachable in production.
nodes.norm_label: the sandbox gateway is not a bypass

nodes.label: No Configured Provider Means No Checkout Method
nodes.rationale: With no Razorpay or Cashfree credentials configuredPaymentProviders() returns an empty list and checkout has nothing to offer. That is the safety property working, not a bug.
nodes.norm_label: no configured provider means no checkout method

nodes.label: Job Endpoints Guarded by a Constant-Time Shared Secret
nodes.rationale: Guarded by CRON_SECRET rather than a session, compared in constant time, and each answers both POST and GET because most hosted schedulers only issue GET.
nodes.norm_label: job endpoints guarded by a constant-time shared secret

nodes.label: Split Cron Cadence (Vercel Floor + GitHub Actions Real Cadence)
nodes.rationale: Vercel Hobby allows two crons firing at most once daily — enough for reconciliation, useless for delivery release. GitHub Actions' 5-minute minimum matches what the release job needs; the daily Vercel crons remain as a floor so a disabled workflow degrades into 'late' rather than 'stopped'.
nodes.norm_label: split cron cadence (vercel floor + github actions real cadence)

nodes.label: A Duplicated Scheduler Run Is a No-Op, Never a Double Delivery
nodes.rationale: release_due_deliveries locks rows with SKIP LOCKED and is idempotent, the dispatcher drains a queue, and reconciliation only records findings — so running both schedulers is safe.
nodes.norm_label: a duplicated scheduler run is a no-op, never a double delivery

nodes.label: vercel.json Pins framework=nextjs
nodes.rationale: It overrides the dashboard Application Preset; with the preset on Other, Vercel runs no Next build and every path returns 404: NOT_FOUND. A 404 on a fresh root path almost always means the preset, not the application.

nodes.label: Environment Variables Validated at Boot
nodes.rationale: The app fails with a readable list so a missing variable is loud rather than mysterious.

nodes.label: Capability States: integrated / mocked / blocked
nodes.rationale: The Owner's integration health view reports these verbatim so the UI never implies a connection the system does not have; moving a row from blocked to integrated switches a path on.

nodes.label: Two Schema Application Routes (db push vs schema.sql)
nodes.rationale: db push keeps migration history and is preferred; the concatenated bundle exists so the schema can be applied with dashboard access alone.
nodes.norm_label: two schema application routes (db push vs schema.sql)

nodes.label: Design Tokens as Single Source of Truth
nodes.rationale: Components use Tailwind theme names (bg-brand, text-ink) and never raw hex; extend tokens in globals.css instead, so a palette change is one file.
nodes.norm_label: design tokens as single source of truth

nodes.label: Two Registers: Storefront Light, Operations Dark
nodes.rationale: One token system; [data-surface="ops"] set by the KOT screens flips the variables. Components are surface-agnostic, so no component needs to know which screen it is on.
nodes.norm_label: two registers: storefront light, operations dark

nodes.label: Order-Source Colors Fixed by the PRD (SourceTag)
nodes.rationale: sw orange, zm red, sx navy, always paired with the literal prefix and never used as decoration — SourceTag is the only place source colors appear.
nodes.norm_label: order-source colors fixed by the prd (sourcetag)

nodes.label: Typography: One Family, Tabular Figures, Ops Sizes Up
nodes.rationale: Geist Sans for everything and Geist Mono for ticket codes and tabular data; ops screens use h-12 buttons and text-lg ticket codes for arm's-length reading.
nodes.norm_label: typography: one family, tabular figures, ops sizes up

nodes.label: Button Family Sharing buttonClasses
nodes.rationale: Button, ButtonLink and ConfirmButton share one class definition in ui/button-styles.ts so they cannot drift.

nodes.label: ConfirmButton — Two-Click Destructive Submit
nodes.rationale: First click arms and turns danger-red, second submits, 4s timeout or blur disarms. Every delete/retire/disable uses it (PRD 19).

nodes.label: Server-Action Feedback via the Query String
nodes.rationale: A server action cannot return a value to a server-rendered page, so outcomes travel back through fail()/done() and <ActionFeedback>; readable() turns Postgres error codes into sentences.
nodes.norm_label: server-action feedback via the query string

nodes.label: Unavailable Product Is Shown, Not Hidden
nodes.rationale: Grayscale image plus an 'Unavailable' badge rather than disappearing, so the catalog does not silently shrink (PRD 6, PRD 19).
nodes.norm_label: unavailable product is shown, not hidden

nodes.label: Money Never Renders on Kitchen Surfaces
nodes.rationale: The views mask it and the UI must not reintroduce it — the design rule mirrors the database guarantee rather than replacing it.
nodes.norm_label: money never renders on kitchen surfaces

nodes.label: Motion Budget and prefers-reduced-motion Kill-Switch
nodes.rationale: 150-250ms color/opacity transitions plus a ck-flash one-shot pulse when a ticket changes for realtime visibility; no page-load choreography.

nodes.label: Layout: Storefront, Admin and KOT Kanban
nodes.rationale: KOT uses full-width Kanban columns under data-surface="ops" with a 44px minimum touch target.
nodes.norm_label: layout: storefront, admin and kot kanban

nodes.label: KOT State Machine (NEW → COMPLETED)
nodes.source_location: the KOT state machine is enforced by the database
nodes.rationale: Legal transitions live in the kot_transitions table, so skipping a step or going backwards is refused by the database rather than by a UI guard.

nodes.label: A Repeated Transition Is a No-Op, Not an Error
nodes.source_location: treats a repeated transition as a no-op
nodes.rationale: A double tap on a kitchen tablet under rush should not surface a failure.
nodes.norm_label: a repeated transition is a no-op, not an error

nodes.label: Rejection Requires a Reason and Confirmation
nodes.source_location: requires a reason before a rejection is accepted
nodes.rationale: kot_transitions.requires_confirmation is true for NEW -> REJECTED, so the two-click UI rule is backed by a data flag.
nodes.norm_label: rejection requires a reason and confirmation

nodes.label: Per-Role Transition Rights on the Board
nodes.rationale: Manager accepts and marks ready; Kitchen only starts preparation; Owner may do neither. The kitchen tells the Manager verbally, so the Manager owns the ready transition.
nodes.norm_label: per-role transition rights on the board

nodes.label: Manager-Only ETA Override Preserving the Original
nodes.source_location: lets only the Manager override a preparation ETA
nodes.rationale: prep_eta_minutes_original survives the override and eta_overridden_by records who changed it, so the kitchen's own estimate is never lost.
nodes.norm_label: manager-only eta override preserving the original

nodes.label: A Status Event for Every Move, Including Creation
nodes.rationale: Each event carries the actor_role, and accepted_at/ready_at are the timestamps prep time is measured from (PRD 10).
nodes.norm_label: a status event for every move, including creation

nodes.label: Source-Prefixed Daily KOT Numbering
nodes.rationale: Each source numbers independently and resets to 001 per business day, kept separate from the monotonic order_number, so the kitchen calls short codes aloud without collisions.

nodes.label: Ticket Priority and SLA Urgency Escalation
nodes.rationale: Marketplace orders start above subscription deliveries because a platform SLA is contractual, and urgency_score escalates to 1000 once sla_due_at passes.
nodes.norm_label: ticket priority and sla urgency escalation

nodes.label: A Ticket Cannot Exist Without a Confirmed Order
nodes.source_location: a ticket cannot exist without a confirmed order
nodes.rationale: Tested by writing straight into the table and bypassing every helper, because the trigger is what has to hold.
nodes.norm_label: a ticket cannot exist without a confirmed order

nodes.label: An Unverified Payment Creates Nothing
nodes.rationale: A declined payment leaves the subscription pending_payment with zero deliveries and zero tickets; a direct UPDATE to active is refused by the 0008 trigger — the last line of defence must hold on its own.

nodes.label: Confirmation Refused Without a Verified Signature
nodes.source_location: refuses to confirm a payment whose signature was not verified
nodes.norm_label: confirmation refused without a verified signature

nodes.label: Uncertain Outcomes Routed to Reconciliation, Not Guessed
nodes.source_location: records an uncertain outcome for reconciliation
nodes.rationale: A gateway TIMEOUT sets needs_reconciliation rather than assuming success or failure, because guessing either way is a money bug.
nodes.norm_label: uncertain outcomes routed to reconciliation, not guessed

nodes.label: Retried Checkout Replays the Original Subscription
nodes.rationale: The same idempotency key returns replayed=true with the same subscription_id and payment_id, and exactly one payments row.
nodes.norm_label: retried checkout replays the original subscription

nodes.label: A Duplicate Payment Webhook Is a No-Op
nodes.source_location: treats a duplicate payment webhook as a no-op
nodes.rationale: The credit grant, the invoice and the coupon redemption each happen exactly once despite two confirmations.
nodes.norm_label: a duplicate payment webhook is a no-op

nodes.label: A Late Failure Notice Cannot Undo a Confirmed Payment
nodes.source_location: will not let a late failure notice undo a confirmed payment
nodes.rationale: Gateway callbacks arrive out of order, so a failure notice against a successful payment is ignored rather than applied.
nodes.norm_label: a late failure notice cannot undo a confirmed payment

nodes.label: No Client Write Policy on payments
nodes.source_location: payment state is separate from order state
nodes.rationale: RLS matches no rows, so a customer UPDATE affects zero rows rather than throwing — the meaningful assertion is that nothing changed, not that it errored.
nodes.norm_label: no client write policy on payments

nodes.label: Invoices Carry a CGST/SGST Tax Split
nodes.rationale: Phase 1 assumes 5% split CGST 2.5% + SGST 2.5%, recorded as separate components and flagged provisional pending owner sign-off.
nodes.norm_label: invoices carry a cgst/sgst tax split

nodes.label: Credit Balance Derived From Ledger Entries
nodes.rationale: The balance is summed from entries rather than held in a mutable column, and the ledger is append-only, so an entitlement is auditable rather than assertable.
nodes.norm_label: credit balance derived from ledger entries

nodes.label: Premium Meals Cost More Credits
nodes.source_location: charges a premium meal more credits

nodes.label: Booking Guards: Balance and Meal Availability
nodes.source_location: will not let a booking exceed the available balance
nodes.rationale: schedule_credit_delivery refuses an overdraft and refuses an unavailable meal, leaving the balance untouched.
nodes.norm_label: booking guards: balance and meal availability

nodes.label: Skipping Returns Credits as a Compensating Entry
nodes.rationale: A 'reverse' entry, not an edit — and repeating the skip is a no-op. A delivery already released to the kitchen can no longer be skipped, because the food is being cooked.
nodes.norm_label: skipping returns credits as a compensating entry

nodes.label: Configured Pause Limits (Length and Count)
nodes.rationale: Both limits are read from business_settings and take effect at runtime; the rule is provisional pending owner sign-off (PRD 22), so it must be retunable without a code change. Deliveries falling inside the pause window are auto-skipped.

nodes.label: Cancellation Stops Future Deliveries but Preserves the Record
nodes.rationale: Scheduled deliveries drop to zero while anything already released to the kitchen is untouched.
nodes.norm_label: cancellation stops future deliveries but preserves the record

nodes.label: Customer-Selected Plans Are Bounded by a Selectable Pool
nodes.rationale: Checkout refuses a meal not selectable on the plan, validated server-side rather than only in the picker UI.
nodes.norm_label: customer-selected plans are bounded by a selectable pool

nodes.label: Marketplace Orders Join the Same KOT
nodes.source_location: marketplace orders join the same KOT
nodes.rationale: ingest_marketplace_order creates a source-prefixed ticket at marketplace priority and stores the external id alongside our own order_number.
nodes.norm_label: marketplace orders join the same kot

nodes.label: Duplicate Marketplace Delivery Is Harmless
nodes.rationale: A replayed webhook event and a repeat without an event id both resolve to the same order and the same single ticket.

nodes.label: Platform-Driven Cancellation Overrides Our Flow
nodes.rationale: A cancel arriving mid-preparation cancels the ticket with cancellation_origin='marketplace'; a status for an unknown order is recorded as a discrepancy, never as a new order.

nodes.label: Per-Provider Circuit Breaker
nodes.source_location: one marketplace failing does not stop the other
nodes.rationale: Consecutive failures past integration.failure_threshold open the circuit for that provider only; a success closes it, and the account reports 'disabled' rather than 'connected' because it has no verified credentials — the honest state.

nodes.label: Two-Way Marketplace Reconciliation
nodes.rationale: Reports orders the platform has that we do not and vice versa, returning 'clean' only when both sides agree.

nodes.label: Capability Honesty: No Unverified 'integrated' State
nodes.rationale: Every capability is integrated, mocked or blocked, and no row may be 'integrated' with verified_at null.

nodes.label: Credentials Stored Only by Reference
nodes.rationale: credentials_ref and webhook_secret_ref hold the NAME of an environment variable, never a secret value, so a database dump leaks no keys.

nodes.label: Role Permissions Are Data, Not Code
nodes.source_location: role permissions are data, not code
nodes.rationale: role_permissions rows define what each role may do, so a permission change is a row change rather than a deploy.
nodes.norm_label: role permissions are data, not code

nodes.label: The Audit Log Cannot Be Rewritten
nodes.rationale: Append-only even to service_role and Developer Admin — an audit trail a privileged actor can edit proves nothing.
nodes.norm_label: the audit log cannot be rewritten

nodes.label: Audit Visibility Limited to Owner and Developer Admin
nodes.rationale: Invisible to the Branch Manager and Kitchen Staff, who work on shared devices.
nodes.norm_label: audit visibility limited to owner and developer admin

nodes.label: Kitchen Money Masking in v_kot_tickets
nodes.source_location: kitchen staff are kept away from money
nodes.rationale: Totals and customer phone come back NULL for kitchen and populated for the Owner from the same view; analytics views and the orders table return zero rows to kitchen.

nodes.label: Customers See and Act Only on Their Own Records
nodes.source_location: customers see only their own records
nodes.rationale: One customer cannot cancel another's subscription; a customer may still update their own name.
nodes.norm_label: customers see and act only on their own records

nodes.label: Self-Promotion to Owner Is Blocked
nodes.source_location: stops a user promoting themselves to Owner
nodes.rationale: A user may not change their own role, closing the most direct privilege-escalation path.

nodes.label: Anonymous Storefront Access Boundary
nodes.rationale: anon may browse published products including unavailable ones and only publicly visible coupons, and reads nothing from customers, orders, payments, subscriptions or audit_logs.

nodes.label: Job: Release Due Deliveries Into the KOT
nodes.rationale: Runs every 5 minutes; releases whatever is due whenever it next runs rather than assuming it was punctual, because GitHub's scheduler is best-effort.
nodes.norm_label: job: release due deliveries into the kot

nodes.label: Job: Drain the Notification Outbox
nodes.rationale: Runs with if: always() so a notification provider being down never hides a release failure.

nodes.label: Concurrency Group Prevents Delayed Runs Piling Up
nodes.norm_label: concurrency group prevents delayed runs piling up

nodes.label: One Transaction Per Migration File
nodes.rationale: Each file commits or rolls back on its own and is recorded in supabase_migrations.schema_migrations so the Supabase CLI recognises it later; a failure stops the run with the Postgres where/detail rather than a half-applied schema.

nodes.label: schema.sql Is Generated, Never Edited
nodes.rationale: Edit the migrations and regenerate; the bundle exists so the schema can be applied with dashboard access alone.

nodes.label: Database-Driven Imagery Constrained by a Host Allowlist
nodes.rationale: Product imagery is database-driven (PRD 13), so the host allowlist is what constrains it rather than any hardcoded asset path.
nodes.norm_label: database-driven imagery constrained by a host allowlist

nodes.label: Rule: Read node_modules/next/dist/docs Before Writing Next.js Code
nodes.rationale: This Next.js version has breaking changes against model training data, so the shipped docs are authoritative over recall.
nodes.norm_label: rule: read node_modules/next/dist/docs before writing next.js code
